title: The crews of HMS Hecla and Griper cutting into Winter Harbour, 26 September 1819
credit: plate engraved by William Westall for Parry 1821, after F. W. Beechey
creator: William Westall, after a sketch by Lieut. F. W. Beechey
description: Both ships' companies sawing and warping a canal more than two miles long through seven inches of new ice to reach the shelter of Winter Harbour on Melville Island. The work took three days, 24 to 26 September 1819. William Edward Parry set every officer and man in both ships to the saws; the plate was engraved after a sketch by Lieutenant Frederick William Beechey, who was aboard the Hecla.

title: H.M. Ships Hecla and Griper in Winter Harbour
credit: National Library of Norway; plate by William Westall after F. W. Beechey, from Parry 1821
creator: William Westall, after a sketch by Lieut. F. W. Beechey
description: The two ships housed over for the winter of 1819-20 at Melville Island, topmasts struck, banked round with snow, under the stars of the polar night. The first European ships deliberately to winter in the high Arctic archipelago.

title: Charles Des Voeux, mate of the Erebus, daguerreotyped at Greenhithe, May 1845
credit: Studio of Richard Beard, 1845; Wikimedia Commons
creator: Studio of Richard Beard
description: One of fourteen sixth-plate daguerreotypes taken in Beard's studio in the days before the ships sailed, hand-tinted with shell gold on the buttons and hat band. Des Voeux was second mate of the Erebus; two years later he signed the Victory Point record with Graham Gore, and by April 1848 he was dead. These plates are the only photographs of any member of the expedition.

title: Dive control aboard the barge Qiniqtiryuaq over the wreck of the Erebus, 6 September 2019
credit: Photograph by Kerry Raymond, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
creator: Kerry Raymond
description: The dive control container on Parks Canada's support barge, moored over the Erebus in Wilmot and Crampton Bay. A diver in a drysuit waits beside the decompression chamber that the remoteness of the site makes necessary. Position is the centre of the protected area; Parks Canada does not publish the wreck's exact coordinates.

title: Roald Amundsen aboard the Gjoa, April 1903
credit: Anders Beer Wilse, hand-coloured lantern slide, 1903; via Wikimedia Commons
creator: Anders Beer Wilse
description: Hand-coloured slide inscribed, in the image, Roald Amundsen ombord Gjoa. April 1903 - taken in Christiania two months before the ship sailed. Photographer and date from the file's own EXIF.

title: Elisha Kent Kane in Arctic gear
credit: National Portrait Gallery, Smithsonian Institution, NPG.2005.38 (CC0); via Wikimedia Commons
creator: unidentified artist
description: A sixth-plate ambrotype of about 1855, made after Kane came home from Smith Sound and while Arctic Explorations was in the press. He was dead within two years. Full-size original, 1854 by 2119 pixels.

title: Amundsen's cabin, 1906
credit: National Library of Norway (Nasjonalbiblioteket), Roald Amundsen photograph collection, no-nb_bldsa_NPRA3119
description: The commander's cabin. Nansen's portrait hung on its wall; Amundsen stopped in front of it on his way on deck the morning the Charles Hanson was sighted.

title: Roald Amundsen, portrait, 1906
credit: National Library of Norway (Nasjonalbiblioteket), Roald Amundsen photograph collection, no-nb_bldsa_NPRA0067
description: Amundsen at the end of the voyage, aged thirty-four.

title: CCGS Amundsen
credit: Cephas, 2011; Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
creator: Cephas
description: The Canadian Coast Guard medium icebreaker named for Roald Amundsen, on the St Lawrence between Quebec City and Levis, 8 March 2011. Launched in 1978 as the Sir John Franklin, laid up in 2000, converted at Les Mechins and recommissioned as CCGS Amundsen on 26 August 2003 as a dedicated Arctic research vessel - ninety-eight years to the day after the Gjoa completed the Northwest Passage. She is the ship this dashboard runs on. REPLACES an earlier file of unknown provenance (amundsen-gjoa-ccgs-amundsen.jpg) which is still on disk and must not be republished; this one is the 2493x1662 Commons original with a named author and a licence.

title: Charles Francis Hall, the only known photograph
credit: Unknown photographer; via Visions of the North (Russell Potter), Wikimedia Commons
creator: photographer unknown
description: Charles Francis Hall, photographed at Washington in the winter of 1870, while he was lobbying Congress for the ship that became the Polaris. The only photograph of him known to exist. Full-size original, 1675 by 2061 pixels.

title: The Polaris
credit: Wood engraving published in Harper's Weekly, May 1873; Wikimedia Commons
creator: unknown engraver, Harper's Weekly
description: The ship as Harper's Weekly showed her to American readers in May 1873, in the weeks the news of Hall's death and the floe drift was reaching the United States.

title: The funeral of Captain Charles Francis Hall
credit: The Frozen Zone and its Explorers (1874); Internet Archive Book Images via Wikimedia Commons
creator: engraving in The Frozen Zone and its Explorers
description: The burial party for Charles Francis Hall at Thank God Harbour, 11 November 1871, in the dark of the polar night: they carried lanterns. A copper cylinder holding the history of the expedition was put into the grave. Full-size original, 3528 by 2176 pixels.

title: The crew of the Polaris
credit: McKenney & Parsons; Library and Archives Canada, via Wikimedia Commons - LAC does not allow free use of works it holds copyright in; verify rights before reuse
licence: public domain (LAC holding: check reuse terms)
creator: McKenney and Parsons (Sherburn Tilton McKenney and Simeon H. Parsons)
description: A group photograph of the Polaris company, 1873, among them George Emory Tyson, the sailing master Sidney O. Buddington and the expedition's scientific chief Emil Bessels.

title: Taking possession of Baffin Island, 9 November 1906
credit: Library and Archives Canada / PA-165672
licence: public domain (Crown copyright expired); LAC images on Wikimedia Commons approved for use by the project owner, request 21
creator: unknown photographer, Dominion Government Arctic expedition
description:
A large group of Inuit and the crew of the C.G.S. Arctic at the ceremony at which Bernier took formal possession of Baffin Island, at the wintering anchorage of Albert Harbour near Mittimatalik (Pond Inlet), on the King's birthday. The photograph is the plainest statement of how these claims were made: a flag, a document in a bottle, and the people who already lived there standing round to watch. Bernier's own account of the day says he told the assembled Inuit "that they had become Canadians".

Library and Archives Canada, accession PA-165672; on Wikimedia Commons as File:Prise de possession de la Terre de Baffin - 9 novembre 1906.jpg. Reuse cleared under the project's standing approval for Library and Archives Canada images already on Commons (request 21).

title: Bernier and the crew of the Arctic at Winter Harbour, Dominion Day 1909
credit: Library and Archives Canada / C-001198
licence: public domain (Crown copyright expired); LAC images on Wikimedia Commons approved for use by the project owner, request 21
creator: unknown photographer, Dominion Government Arctic expedition
description:
The ship's company gathered at Parry's Rock at Winter Harbour on Melville Island on 1 July 1909 for the unveiling of the tablet claiming the whole Arctic Archipelago for Canada. The rock behind them carries the names Parry's men cut in 1820; see [[topic:ross-parry]]. Library and Archives Canada dates the photograph to the winter of 1908-09 at Winter Harbour; Commons gives the day of the ceremony, 1 July 1909, which is what the report describes.

Library and Archives Canada, copy negative C-001198; LAC record 3652544. On Wikimedia Commons as File:Capitaine Joseph-Elzear Bernier et son equipage a Winter Harbour.jpg. Reuse cleared under the project's standing approval for Library and Archives Canada images already on Commons (request 21).

title: The Roosevelt at Cape Sheridan
credit: plate from Henson, A Negro Explorer at the North Pole (1912)
creator: Matthew Henson
description: Peary's ship banked in at the north-east corner of Ellesmere Island, the northernmost point a vessel had reached under her own power. From here the sledge parties went west along the shore to Cape Columbia and out onto the sea ice.

title: The Nascopie in the ice
credit: Hudson's Bay Company Heritage, via Wikimedia Commons; public domain in Canada
creator: photographer unknown
description: The supply ship stopped in heavy ice, undated but from her working years between 1912 and 1946. This is the largest copy on Commons, 960 by 380 pixels; the Hudson's Bay Company's own heritage pages are given as its source.

title: A rowing boat alongside the Nascopie at Mittimatalik, 1938
credit: Lorene Squire (1908-1942), Hudson's Bay Company, via Wikimedia Commons; public domain
creator: Lorene Squire
description: Ship day at Pond Inlet: a boat pulling out to the Nascopie on her one annual call. Lorene Squire was an American wildlife photographer who travelled the eastern Arctic with the Hudson's Bay Company in 1938; she was killed in a car accident in 1942. Only a small copy exists on Commons, 453 by 452 pixels; a larger print may be held by the Hudson's Bay Company Archives.

title: Inuit women in new parkas waiting for the Nascopie's passengers
credit: Library and Archives Canada / BiblioArchives, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0
creator: Library and Archives Canada
description: The other side of ship day. Library and Archives Canada's caption: Inuit women in new parkas awaiting the arrival of passengers from the RMS Nascopie. Neither the place nor the year is given by the archive; pinned provisionally at Mittimatalik and dated loosely to the 1930s, when the Nascopie carried the Eastern Arctic Patrol. A larger original will be in the LAC fonds.

title: Alert and Discovery leaving Portsmouth for the Arctic, 29 May 1875
credit: Watercolour by Lt Francis Henry Boyer RN, 1875; public domain via Wikimedia Commons
creator: Francis Henry Boyer
description: The two ships of the British Arctic Expedition just off the Isle of Wight on the afternoon of 29 May 1875, painted by a young officer of the Royal Navy. Nares had a telegram from the Queen in his pocket wishing him and his gallant companions every success.

title: The Alert nipped near Cape Beechey, Robeson Channel
credit: Photograph by Thomas Mitchell and George White; plate from Nares, Narrative of a Voyage to the Polar Sea (1878); public domain
creator: Thomas Mitchell and George White
description: One of the earliest photographs taken of a ship in the ice above 81 degrees north. Mitchell, paymaster of the Discovery, and White, assistant engineer of the Alert, made most of the expedition's photographs with wet plates in temperatures that froze their chemicals.

title: HMS Alert about to winter off Floeberg Beach, October 1875
credit: Painting by J. Hamer; public domain via Wikimedia Commons (Christie's LotFinder 102661)
creator: J. Hamer
description: The Alert banked in for the winter behind grounded floebergs at 82 deg 27 min N, the highest latitude at which any ship had wintered. The crew saw no sun for 142 days. Dated to October 1875 by the painting's own title.

title: Henry Wemyss Feilden, naturalist of HMS Alert
credit: Norfolk Museums Service polar collections; public domain via Wikimedia Commons
creator: unknown photographer
description: Feilden collected the geology, birds and fossil plants of the coasts above 82 degrees, the first systematic natural history of the region. Undated portrait; pinned to the Alert's winter quarters.

title: Hans Hendrik with his family on the upper deck of HMS Discovery, 20 July 1875
credit: Photograph by Thomas Mitchell; Royal Museums Greenwich P39584; public domain via Wikimedia Commons
creator: Thomas Mitchell
description: Taken at Proven (Kangersuatsiaq), Greenland, where the ships lay from 19 to 21 July 1875 to engage Inuit dog drivers. Hans Hendrik of Fiskenaesset had already served Kane, Hayes and Hall; this was his fourth expedition. He is shown with two of his children. The Royal Museums Greenwich catalogue labels the third figure a daughter or wife, uncertainly. See [[topic:kane-hall-polaris]].

title: Members of the Lady Franklin Bay Expedition before sailing, 1881
credit: Photograph by Moses Parker Rice, 1881; NOAA Arctic Research Office; public domain
creator: Moses Parker Rice
description: The American members of the expedition photographed before they left for the north in June 1881. Dr. Pavy's head was pasted into the print later because he joined at Godhavn, and three other portraits were altered when the party changed. Twenty-three men are shown; nineteen of the twenty-five who wintered would die. Pinned to Baltimore, from which the expeditionary force sailed.

title: The steam launch Lady Greely in Discovery Harbour, August 1882
credit: Photograph by Sgt George W. Rice, August 1882; Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division, LCCN 2006676094
creator: George W. Rice
description: The launch Lockwood christened for Greely's wife, towing a small boat in Discovery Harbour. She fetched the two Greenlandic drivers from Proven in July 1881, worked the fiords for two summers, and towed three boats out of Fort Conger on the retreat of 9 August 1883. Sergeant Cross was her engineer.

title: The Proteus on the morning of the day she was crushed, 23 July 1883
credit: NOAA Arctic Research Office, First International Polar Year collection; public domain
description: The sealer that had carried the expedition north in 1881, held in the ice of Kane Basin on the morning of 23 July 1883. She was nipped and sank the same evening, taking most of the relief stores with her and leaving Greely to a second winter with nothing sent to him. Position approximate.

title: The Thetis and Bear stopped by ice south of the Duck Islands, 6 June 1884
credit: NOAA Arctic Research Office, First International Polar Year collection; public domain
description: Schley's two relief ships held up in the Melville Bay pack on 6 June 1884, sixteen days before they reached Cape Sabine. No relief squadron had attempted Melville Bay so early in the season. Position approximate, off the west Greenland coast.

title: Canadian Forces Station Alert, May 2016
credit: Photograph by Kevin Rawlings, 30 May 2016, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons
creator: Kevin Rawlings
description: The northernmost permanently inhabited place in the world, a few kilometres from the beach where Nares's Alert lay through the winter of 1875-76 and from which the station takes its name. Alert now keeps one of the longest atmospheric baseline records in the Arctic. See [[topic:science-stations]].

title: The whaler Alert in sailing ice
credit: Lewis, The Life and Work of the Rev. E. J. Peck among the Eskimos (1904); Internet Archive copy lifeworkofrevejp00lewiuoft
creator: photographer unknown
description: Crawford Noble's whaler Alert, the ship that carried Peck and Parker to Cumberland Sound in the summer of 1894 and that was holed by ice in a gale on her way back to the island in September. Pinned in Davis Strait off Cape Mercy, where Peck first sighted land on 18 August 1894. Rendered at 300 dpi from the Internet Archive's scan, page 245 of the PDF.

title: The CCGS Amundsen in the ice, 5 June 2008
credit: Photograph by Tatiana Pichugina, 5 June 2008, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons (originally on Flickr)
creator: Tatiana Pichugina
description: The ship during the International Polar Year, in the year she spent overwintering in the Beaufort Sea for the Circumpolar Flaw Lead study. The position given is the centre of that study area, not the exact spot the photograph was taken.

title: First discovery of land by H.M.S. Investigator, 6 September 1850
credit: Christie's / Wikimedia Commons; after Cresswell 1854, plate I
creator: Samuel Gurney Cresswell; lithographed by William Simpson
description: Plate I of Cresswell's series. The Investigator, six weeks through Bering Strait, raises the high land of Baring Island (Banks Island) on 6 September 1850 in what is now Amundsen Gulf. The position is approximate, taken from the ship's track for that day rather than from the plate.

title: H.M.S. Investigator in the pack, 8 October 1850
credit: Special Collections, Toronto Public Library (br 919.8 c67 plate III), via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0
licence: CC BY-SA 2.0 (scan); the 1854 lithograph is public domain
creator: Samuel Gurney Cresswell
description: Plate III. The ship fast in the moving pack at the head of Prince of Wales Strait in October 1850, drifting with the floe. It was from this besetment that the sledge party set out that saw the coast of Melville Island.

title: Critical position of H.M.S. Investigator on the north coast of Baring Island, 20 August 1851
credit: Toronto Public Library / Royal Geographical Society, via Wikimedia Commons
creator: Samuel Gurney Cresswell
description: Plate IV, the best known of the series. In August 1851 the Investigator, working north along the exposed west coast of Banks Island, was squeezed between the grounded ice and the cliffs; the crew had provisions and boats on the floe ready to abandon her. Position approximate.

title: Sledge party leaving H.M.S. Investigator in Mercy Bay, 15 April 1853
credit: Library and Archives Canada, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0
licence: CC BY 2.0 (scan); the 1854 lithograph is public domain
creator: Samuel Gurney Cresswell
description: Plate VII, drawn by the man who led the party. On 15 April 1853 Cresswell took the sick and the weakest of the crew away from the ship across the ice of Mercy Bay towards Melville Island. Going on from there to Beechey Island and home in 1853, he was the first man to pass from the Pacific side to the Atlantic side of the North-West Passage.

title: The Phoenix and the Breadalbane landing stores at Cape Riley
credit: Illustrated London News; Wikimedia Commons
creator: Frederick James Smyth, wood engraver
description: The only contemporary picture of the Breadalbane, engraved for the Illustrated London News and published on 22 October 1853, two months after she went down. The two ships lie off Cape Riley, next door to Beechey Island, working stores onto the beach; the coal landed here was still on the shingle when she was lost, and could not be recovered. Original upload 1200 by 853 pixels.

title: The St. Roch preserved at the Vancouver Maritime Museum
credit: Roy Luck, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
creator: Roy Luck
description: The hull under her A-frame at Kitsilano Point, restored to her 1944 appearance. 3168 by 4752 pixels, the original upload.

title: The St. Roch in winter quarters at Herschel Island
credit: Library and Archives Canada, PA-202182
creator: Jules-Ernest Livernois
description: The RCMP patrol vessel housed over for the winter at Qikiqtaruk (Herschel Island) in the Beaufort Sea, the anchorage she used on both passages. The canvas housing over the deck is what Larsen describes: without it the fine drifting snow finds every crack.

title: H.M.S. Investigator running through a narrow channel in a snow storm, 23 September 1851
credit: Special Collections, Toronto Public Library, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0
licence: CC BY-SA 2.0 (scan); the 1854 lithograph is public domain
creator: Samuel Gurney Cresswell
description: Plate V. The ship driving between grounded and packed ice in a snowstorm on the north coast of Banks Land, the night before she went aground and then found the Bay of Mercy. Position approximate.

title: The perilous situation of H.M.S. Investigator while wintering in the pack, 1850-51
credit: Royal Museums Greenwich, PZ6687, via Wikimedia Commons
creator: Edward Augustus Inglefield, after S. Gurney Cresswell
description: A separate plate, after Cresswell and dedicated to McClure, of the first winter in the pack in Prince of Wales Strait. The original is a large scan held by the Royal Museums Greenwich; the 32 MB TIFF is kept here rather than a derived copy.

title: The Karluk survivors on board the Bear
credit: Bartlett and Hale, The Last Voyage of the Karluk (1916), via Wikimedia Commons
description: Munro, Hadley, Captain Bartlett, Kiruk (Keruk), McKinlay, Chafe, Williams, Williamson and Helen, photographed after the rescue. Kiruk made the clothing that every one of them walked off the ice in; Helen was seven and had walked the whole way from Shipwreck Camp.

title: The drift of the Karluk
credit: Bartlett and Hale, The Last Voyage of the Karluk (1916), via Wikimedia Commons
description: The chart printed in Bartlett's book showing the ship's track from Point Barrow east to Camden Bay, the eleven-month drift west and north to latitude 73, and the sinking north of Herald Island. Compare [[artifact:karluk-cae-001]].

title: The Karluk in her whaling years
credit: Bartlett and Hale, The Last Voyage of the Karluk (1916), via Wikimedia Commons
description: The brigantine that became the expedition's flagship, photographed before 1913. She was built in 1884 for the Aleutian cod fishery, converted for whaling, and was thirty-nine years old and not an ice ship when Bartlett took her north.

title: Stefansson's party leaving the Karluk
credit: Bartlett and Hale, The Last Voyage of the Karluk (1916), via Wikimedia Commons
description: The caribou hunt of 20 September 1913, photographed from the ship. A gale that night took the Karluk west, and the six men on the ice never saw her again. It is the most argued-over photograph in this topic.

title: Unloading the Mary Sachs at Cape Kellett
credit: Canadian Museum of History, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)
creator: George Hubert Wilkins
description: Two men carrying a load ashore from the schooner on 1 September 1914, ten days before Stefansson walked in from the ice and found the base existed. The community of Sachs Harbour on Banks Island is named for this ship. Canadian Museum of History negative 50855.

title: Resolute, Assistance, Intrepid and Pioneer wintering, 1850-51
credit: Wikimedia Commons, from a Christie's sale image; attributed to W. H. J. Browne; public domain
creator: attributed to William Henry James Browne RN
description: Austin's four ships - Resolute, Assistance, and the steam tenders Intrepid and Pioneer - housed over on the fixed floe between Griffith Island and Cape Martyr through the winter of 1850-51, attributed to William Henry James Browne, a naval officer who had wintered with James Clark Ross at Port Leopold in 1848-49 and drew several of the best-known views of the search. Horatio Thomas Austin commanded the squadron, Erasmus Ommanney the Assistance and Sherard Osborn the Pioneer; Francis Leopold McClintock was one of the lieutenants. Only a small 512 by 301 pixel reproduction survives in the public file, taken from a saleroom photograph rather than an institutional scan; a larger copy would have to come from the Royal Museums Greenwich or from the original sale catalogue.

title: The Aurora at Cape York, 1884
credit: Lindsay, A Voyage to the Arctic in the Whaler Aurora (Boston: Dana Estes, 1911); Wikimedia Commons, File:FMIB 34359 Aurora at Cape York.jpeg
creator: David Moore Lindsay
description: The Dundee steam whaler Aurora off Cape York, at the top of Melville Bay and the gate of the North Water. This is the landfall a sailing whaler spent three weeks working towards.

title: The Aurora in the nips off Cape York
credit: Lindsay, A Voyage to the Arctic in the Whaler Aurora (Boston: Dana Estes, 1911); Wikimedia Commons, File:FMIB 34381 Aurora in the Nips off Cape York.jpeg
creator: David Moore Lindsay
description: A ship being nipped: the ice closing on both sides and lifting her. Commons records the caption 'From a photo taken at the time'. This is what destroyed nineteen or twenty ships in a week in June 1830, photographed fifty-four years later on a ship that survived it.

title: Alacee Nungaq and three of her children at Resolute Bay, March 1956
credit: Gar Lunney / National Film Board of Canada. Phototheque / Library and Archives Canada / e010949311
licence: CC BY 2.0 (Library and Archives Canada Flickr stream)
pages: identified from the QTC's 1955 family table, p. 30
creator: Gar Lunney
description: Alacee Nungaq - Alici Nungak in the Qikiqtani Truth Commission's table of the 1955 relocatees - photographed by Gar Lunney at Resolute Bay in March 1956, in an amauti with three of her children, five months into the family's second winter. Library and Archives Canada's caption reads: "Inuit woman [Alacee Nungaq] wearing an amauti and three children [Philip, Annie and Anna Levi] outside in Resolute Bay, Northwest Territories." The QTC's table lists Levi Nungak and his wife Alici with their daughters Annie, Minnie and Anna and their son Philipusie; the archive's spelling and the Makivik spelling differ, and the archive has given the children their father's given name as a surname, a habit of the period. Behind them is the settlement on the west shore of Resolute Bay, then a row of houses the families had built from scrap taken off the RCAF dump. It is the one photograph of a family relocated to Qausuittuq that carries a licence permitting reuse. Commons file name: Woman and three children outside in winter clothes Femme et trois enfants a l'exterieur en vetements d'hiver (7342566364).jpg. Position is the old village site and approximate to about 1.5 km.

title: Moss, plate X: the Alert in winter quarters, from among the barrier bergs, March 1876
credit: Edward Lawton Moss, Shores of the Polar Sea (1878), chromolithograph plate, via Wikimedia Commons
creator: Edward Lawton Moss
description: The Alert at Floeberg Beach seen from among the grounded floebergs to seaward, in the sunrise light of March. Moss: 'Nowhere is it more true that the low sun makes the colour than in the Arctic regions. The ice and snow, that are wearily white in midsummer, glow with all sorts of opaline tints in the sunrise light of March.' The Commons file carries no plate number; the plate is identified here as number X from Moss's own description of it, in which the berg in the centre has been worn into columns and alcoves by the surface floods of a former summer and no land shows beyond the ship, which distinguishes it from plate XI.

title: Moss, plate IX: The dawn of 1876, HMS Alert in winter quarters
credit: Edward Lawton Moss, Shores of the Polar Sea (1878), chromolithograph plate, via Wikimedia Commons
creator: Edward Lawton Moss
description: The Alert housed in for the winter at Floeberg Beach, looking north at midnight very early in March 1876. Moss made the outlines with a pencil pushed through two pairs of worsted mitts while the spirit thermometers on the stand and on the tripod at the left of the ship read 70 degrees below zero Fahrenheit; the colours were laid on below decks by candlelight and checked by repeated trips into the cold. The chain cables running away to the left, raised on casks to keep them from sinking into the floe, secured the ship against being blown to sea with the ice. The Commons file carries no plate number; the plate is identified here as number IX from Moss's own description of it, which names the thermometer tripod and the raised cables.

title: Spearing Arctic char
credit: Photograph by David Haig-Thomas, plate in The Geographical Journal 95 (1940); Royal Geographical Society
licence: in copyright; reproduced from the JSTOR scan for research use
creator: David Haig-Thomas
description: An Inughuit fisher in skin trousers leaning over the water with a barbed leister, other spears beside him. Captioned 'Spearing Arctic char'.

title: Arctic hare in Ellesmere Island
credit: Photograph by David Haig-Thomas, plate in The Geographical Journal 95 (1940); Royal Geographical Society
licence: in copyright; reproduced from the JSTOR scan for research use
creator: David Haig-Thomas
description: A white Arctic hare on rock, water and a mountainous shore behind. Haig-Thomas noted that in 1938, but not on his 1935 visit, Arctic hares and lemmings were very numerous and the sides of the fiords were dotted with their tracks - one of the few animal-abundance comparisons the expedition could make across three years.

title: The Signalhorn in loose pack
credit: Oxford University Ellesmere Land Expedition; plate in The Geographical Journal 87 (1936), read from the University of Manitoba's licensed JSTOR copy
licence: in copyright (published 1936); held here for internal research use under the library's licence
creator: Oxford University Ellesmere Land Expedition
description: The chartered Norwegian sealer, 100 tons gross, among loose floes. It was ice like this, and worse, that stopped her twice in Smith Sound in August 1934 and forced the expedition to winter at Etah instead of Fort Conger.

title: Krüger with officers and men of the Beothic, 1929
credit: Photo courtesy National Archives of Canada; Barr 1993, fig. 6
licence: in copyright; reproduced from Polar Record for research
description: Krüger (right) among the ship's people of the Canadian government's eastern Arctic patrol ship Beothic, which carried him north in the summer of 1929 and landed his stores. The caption does not say where the picture was taken; the position given here is Fram Havn, where the Beothic lay on 3 August 1929.

title: Man's prey of the Arctic sea - walrus asleep
credit: Frederick A. Cook, My Attainment of the Pole (1911); scan poleattainment00cookrich, Internet Archive
creator: Frederick A. Cook
description: Walrus asleep on the ice of Smith Sound. Walrus meat and blubber were what the Annoatok camp lived on and what the expedition's pemmican and dog food were made from; a year later, at Cape Sparbo, walrus hide would be the party's chief food and the cause of their broken teeth.

title: Rudolph Francke in Arctic costume
credit: Frederick A. Cook, My Attainment of the Pole (1911); scan poleattainment00cookrich, Internet Archive
creator: Frederick A. Cook
description: Rudolph Franke, the German sailor who was Cook's only white companion, photographed at Annoatok in Inughuit fur dress. Franke was left to hold the box-house and the expedition's stores while Cook was away; he grew ill with scurvy and went south in the summer of 1908, leaving the base and its furs in the hands of Harry Whitney and Peary's people.

title: Along the edge of the polar sea - last land's end
credit: Frederick A. Cook, My Attainment of the Pole (1911); scan poleattainment00cookrich, Internet Archive
creator: Frederick A. Cook
description: The north-west corner of Axel Heiberg Island, where the land stops and the moving ice of the Arctic Ocean begins. Cook reached this point, which he called Svartevoeg and which is now Cape Stallworthy, on 17 March 1908; Sverdrup had named the headland to the north-east Cape Thomas Hubbard in 1900.

title: S.S. "Diana" Loading at Brooklyn Navy-yard
credit: Donald B. MacMillan, Four Years in the White North (New York: Harper, 1918); Internet Archive scan fouryearsinwhite00macm
creator: Donald B. MacMillan
description: The Diana taking in the expedition's stores at the Brooklyn Navy Yard before sailing on 2 July 1913. She struck at Barge Point, Labrador, on 16 July and was condemned at Battle Harbour; the expedition went on north in the Erik.

title: Constructing a Snow House / Our Camp at Cape Isabella, May 1917
credit: Donald B. MacMillan, Four Years in the White North (New York: Harper, 1918); Internet Archive scan fouryearsinwhite00macm
creator: Donald B. MacMillan
description: Two photographs: an igloo going up, "in about one hour our home for the night, consisting of some fifty blocks, will be ready for occupancy"; and the camp at Cape Isabella in May 1917, with the fur coats stowed on top of the igloo out of reach of stray dogs.

title: Bay at his morning toilet
credit: Sverdrup, New Land (Longmans Green, 1904), vol. II, p. 414
description: Edvard Bay, the expedition's zoologist named in the caption, seated on a sledge grooming himself while a companion looks on, from the chapter 'North Devon and Stenkulfjord' describing the sledge party's return after a snow-blind Baumann held them up for two days.

title: William Baffin's chart of Hudson Strait, 1615
credit: Markham 1881, p. 103, via Wikimedia Commons
creator: William Baffin
description: Drawn on the 1615 voyage of the Discovery under Bylot with Baffin as pilot. Baffin worked the strait with tidal observations and lunar-distance longitudes and concluded, correctly, that no passage led west out of it. The chart is the working document behind that judgement.

title: The north of Foxe's card: Baffin Bay, Smith Sound, Jones Sound and Lancaster Sound in print
credit: Princeton University Library scan, via Wikimedia Commons
creator: Luke Foxe
description: A detail of the same card showing the top of the world as 1635 had it: Groonland, Baffins Bay, Sir Thomas Smith, Alderman Iones and Lancaster Sound all lettered in, with Hudsons Bay and Buttons Bay below. Every one of Baffin's 1616 names is here, and within a generation cartographers began dropping them again as unproven. They were not confirmed until John Ross in 1818.

title: Boas's map of the Inuit divisions of Baffin Land and the Hudson Strait coast, 1888
credit: Boas, The Central Eskimo (1888), Plate II; Project Gutenberg ebook 42084
creator: Franz Boas
description: Boas's plate showing in detail the territory of each named group: the Oqomiut and Akudnirmiut of Cumberland Sound and Davis Strait, the Nugumiut of Frobisher Bay, the Tununirmiut of Eclipse Sound and Admiralty Inlet, the Aivilingmiut and Iglulingmiut of Repulse Bay and Lyon Inlet, and the Netsilingmiut of the Boothia isthmus and King William Land. Most of the coastline behind it was not surveyed by Boas; it is Inuit geography, taken from Inuit charts and Inuit directions and checked where he could travel.

title: Michael Lok's chart of 1582, dedicated to Philip Sidney
credit: from Hakluyt, Divers Voyages (1582), plate as reproduced by J. Hyatt
creator: Michael Lok
description: Drawn by the ruined governor of the Cathay Company four years after the last voyage, and printed in Hakluyt's Divers Voyages. 'Frobisher' is written across an open strait north of a large 'Meta Incognita', and the Zeno brothers' phantom island of Frisland floats in mid-Atlantic where Frobisher took Greenland to be. It also carries the earliest surviving map use of the name 'Canada' in an English book. The Commons file name for this scan was not recorded by the run that fetched it.

title: Discoveries in the Arctic Sea, with additions and changes to 1909
credit: Bibliotheque de l'Universite Laval
creator: Joseph-Elzear Bernier
description: Bernier's general chart of the Archipelago as it stood after the 1908-09 voyage, showing the islands Sverdrup's parties had added in the west and the tracks of the Canadian patrols. The Commons original is 24,267 by 19,917 pixels and 1.45 GB; the copy held here is a full-quality 8,000-pixel JPEG made from it, which resolves the lettering. The original can be re-fetched from the download URL if anyone needs it.

title: Voyage of the C.G.S. Arctic, 1908-1909
credit: Bibliotheque de l'Universite Laval
creator: Joseph-Elzear Bernier
description: The track chart of the sovereignty voyage: out through Lancaster Sound and Barrow Strait to M'Clure Strait, the winter at Winter Harbour, and the return by Byam Martin and Austin channels. Held here as a full-quality 8,000-pixel JPEG made from the 249 MB Commons original.

title: Winter Harbour, Melville Island, Arctic Sea, 1909
credit: University of Alberta Libraries via Internet Archive; from Bernier's 1910 report
creator: Joseph-Elzear Bernier
description: A detailed hydrographic survey of the harbour where the Arctic lay through the winter of 1908-09, with soundings in fathoms and the heights of the peaks used for triangulation. It was an early survey made to establish an anchorage that Canada could call its own; Parry's Rock, where the tablet was set on 1 July 1909, is on its shore.

title: Arrowsmith's chart of the Arctic shores of America, 1818-1859
credit: Royal Museums Greenwich, F0157, via Wikimedia Commons; public domain
creator: John Arrowsmith F.R.G.S.
description: The single best summary of what the search put on the chart: a hand-coloured engraved sheet by John Arrowsmith, the Royal Geographical Society's mapmaker, showing the Arctic shores of America from Baffin Bay to Cape Bathurst with the coasts and rivers explored by the British expeditions between 1818 and 1859, principally in search of Franklin. Published in 1860, the year after McClintock came home, so it is the chart of the archipelago as the search left it. The original file is a 6,660 by 5,341 pixel TIFF of 107 MB, held here in full. Worth opening beside a modern chart of the same water: the coastlines are recognisable, the channels between them often are not, and the places where Arrowsmith's engraver simply stopped drawing are the places nobody had walked.

title: NTS 1:250,000 sheet 089B, Intrepid Inlet
credit: Natural Resources Canada, CanMatrix scanned NTS sheet 089B, Open Government Licence - Canada
creator: Surveys and Mapping Branch, Department of Energy, Mines and Resources (successor to the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys)
description: 76-77 N, 116-120 W: the middle of Prince Patrick Island, Intrepid Inlet and Mould Bay, where the joint Canadian-American weather station opened in 1948. The station name was approved 3 April 1949 and the bay itself on 3 March 1949.

title: NTS 1:250,000 sheet 058F, Resolute
credit: Natural Resources Canada, CanMatrix scanned NTS sheet 058F, Open Government Licence - Canada
creator: Surveys and Mapping Branch, Department of Energy, Mines and Resources (successor to the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys)
description: 74-75 N, 92-96 W: Cornwallis Island and Resolute Bay, the airfield and supply base from which most of the high-Arctic flying and later the SHORAN work was staged. The name Resolute Bay was approved on 4 September 1952.

title: Boas's map of the tribes of Baffin Land and their territories, 1888
credit: Franz Boas, The Central Eskimo (Bureau of Ethnology, 1888); Internet Archive
creator: Franz Boas
description: Plate II of The Central Eskimo: the territories of the Oqomiut, Nugumiut, Akudnirmiut, Padlimiut, Sikosuilarmiut, Akuliarmiut, Iglulirmiut, Aivillirmiut and Netchillirmiut, each group named for the place it belonged to. The map is a place-name document as much as an ethnographic one - every group name on it is a place name with -miut, 'the people of', on the end. See [[topic:inuit-oral-history]].

title: The Inuit Heritage Trust's Grise Fiord and Resolute Bay place-names layer
credit: Inuit Heritage Trust Traditional Place Names Program
licence: Inuit Heritage Trust; attribution requested, contact IHT for current data
creator: Inuit Heritage Trust Traditional Place Names Program, with elders and hunters of Ausuittuq and Qausuittuq
description: The KML layer itself: 346 named points across southern Ellesmere, Devon, Cornwallis, Bathurst, Coburg Island and the waters between, each with syllabics, roman orthography, a feature type, an explanation of the name, a position, and the official English name where there is one. Thirty-four carry an official equivalent, which makes them the only verified Inuktitut-to-English concordance for the northern archipelago. Recorded with elders from 2008; the file is dated May 2025. IHT notes that many of the names are not yet official and that there may be errors. The raster view is a plain plot of the 344 placemarks that carry coordinates, made from the KML on this machine, not a map published by the Trust.

title: Baffin Bay and the route north to Thule
credit: HathiTrust page scan (University of Michigan copy) of Haig-Thomas, Tracks in the Snow (Oxford University Press, 1939)
licence: public domain (HathiTrust full view; author died 1941)
creator: drawn for Tracks in the Snow
description: The book's first map: Greenland and Baffin Bay from Cape Farewell to Ellesmere Island, with Jakobshavn, Disko, Umanak, Upernavik, Melville Bay, Thule, Robertson Bay, Bache Peninsula and Craig Harbour marked - the itinerary of the voyage out, drawn at a scale of four hundred miles.

title: Baffin's autograph map of his fourth voyage to the north-west, 1615
credit: Markham (ed.), The Voyages of William Baffin, 1612-1622 (London: Hakluyt Society, 1881); scan Internet Archive
creator: William Baffin
description: Facsimile of the manuscript chart William Baffin drew of the 1615 voyage in the Discovery with Robert Bylot, from British Museum Add. MSS. 12206. The coasts Baffin himself saw are washed in colour, the ship's track is pricked in red, and the unseen shores are left as faint outline - an honest map of what was and was not observed. It covers Hudson Strait, Foxe Channel and the approaches to Southampton Island.

title: Baffin's Bay on five successive charts
credit: Markham (ed.), The Voyages of William Baffin, 1612-1622 (London: Hakluyt Society, 1881); scan Internet Archive
creator: Markham (ed.)
description: A fold-out plate setting five charts of Baffin Bay side by side, from Baffin's own delineation of 1616 through the eighteenth-century blanks to the nineteenth-century surveys - the plate Markham used to argue that Baffin's much-doubted bay had been right all along.

title: Entrance to the Persian Gulf, to illustrate the last voyage of Baffin
credit: Markham (ed.), The Voyages of William Baffin, 1612-1622 (London: Hakluyt Society, 1881); scan Internet Archive
creator: Markham (ed.)
description: Chart of the entrance to the Persian Gulf, showing Qeshm and Ormuz, where Baffin was killed in January 1622 while taking the height of a wall under fire during the East India Company's siege - the end of the navigator who had charted Baffin Bay six years earlier.

title: Plan of Elizabeth Harbour
credit: Ross, Narrative of a Second Voyage in Search of a North-West Passage (London: A. W. Webster, 1835); scan Internet Archive
creator: John Ross
description: A surveyed plan of Elizabeth Harbour on the Boothia coast, with soundings and the bearings taken from the ship.

title: Plan of Felix Harbour, 1830
credit: Ross, Narrative of a Second Voyage in Search of a North-West Passage (London: A. W. Webster, 1835); scan Internet Archive
creator: John Ross
description: The surveyed plan of Felix Harbour where the Victory lay through the first winter, with the ship's berth marked and the soundings taken round her.

title: Sketch map of the Arctic regions at the time of Franklin's last expedition, and the drift of the Fox down Baffin's Bay
credit: McClintock, The Voyage of the 'Fox' in the Arctic Seas (London: John Murray, 1859); scan Internet Archive
creator: Francis Leopold McClintock
description: Two maps on one leaf at the front of McClintock's narrative: what was known of the Arctic when Franklin sailed in 1845, and the track of the Fox as she was carried 1,194 miles south down Baffin Bay in the pack through the winter of 1857-58 before she could begin her search at all.

title: Geological map of the Arctic Islands: title sheet and west portion
credit: Low, Report on the Dominion Government Expedition to Hudson Bay and the Arctic Islands on board the D.G.S. Neptune, 1903-04 (Ottawa: Government Printing Bureau, 1906); scan Internet Archive
creator: C. Frank King
description: Title sheet of the Geological Survey of Canada's map illustrating Low's report, covering the Parry Islands, Ellesmere Island and the central Arctic Archipelago.

title: Sketch map of the Arctic Archipelago
credit: McClintock, The Voyage of the 'Fox' in the Arctic Seas (London: John Murray, 1859); scan Internet Archive
creator: Francis Leopold McClintock
description: The large folding map at the end of Francis Leopold McClintock's narrative, laying out the archipelago as it stood after the Fox's voyage, with the search tracks and the ground covered on King William Island where Franklin's people died. It is the first published chart to show the whole circuit of King William Island, completed by McClintock and Hobson in 1859.

title: Vicinity chart of Station A: Resolution Island, Port Burwell and Cape Chidley
credit: Canada, Report of the Hudson Strait Expedition, 1927-28 (Ottawa: F.A. Acland, 1929); scan Internet Archive
creator: Hudson Strait Expedition
description: Foldout chart (Appendix 3) of the eastern entrance to Hudson Strait around Base A at Port Burwell, plotting the triangular routine air patrols A-I, A-II and A-III flown from the base.

title: Chart of the Polaris Expedition, C. F. Hall commanding
credit: Davis (ed.), Narrative of the North Polar Expedition, U.S. Ship Polaris (Washington: Government Printing Office, 1876); scan Internet Archive
creator: U.S. Navy Hydrographic Office
description: The official chart of the North Polar Expedition under Charles Francis Hall, laying down three separate tracks in different lines: the outward track of the Polaris up Smith Sound to Thank God Harbor, her return, and the drift of the ice-floe party under George Emory Tyson that was carried some fifteen hundred miles south to the Labrador Sea, with the boat party's course.

title: Esquimaux Chart, Drawn by Koojesse
credit: Hall, Life with the Esquimaux (London: Sampson Low, 1864); scan Internet Archive
creator: Koojesse
description: A hand-drawn chart of Frobisher Bay ("Tin-nu-jok-ping-oo-se-ong") and Cumberland Sound (Kin-gaite) made by the Inuit guide Koojesse at Rescue Harbour in 1860 for C. F. Hall, showing the coastline, islands, and Hudson Strait. Hall reproduced it to demonstrate the accuracy of Inuit geographic knowledge.

title: Chart of Greenland, Davis Strait, Cumberland, Frobisher Strait, Hudson Strait and Labrador
credit: Miertsching, Reise-Tagebuch des Missionars Joh. Aug. Miertsching (Gnadau, 1855); scan Internet Archive
creator: Lith. Anst. v. L. Kraatz, Berlin
description: The folding chart in Miertsching's German journal, lithographed in Berlin, showing Cape Farewell, the Davis Strait, Cumberland and Northumberland Inlet, Frobisher Strait, Hudson Strait and the Labrador coast, with the outward route marked.

title: The drift of the Karluk
credit: Internet Archive scan (lastvoyageofkarl00bartuoft) of Bartlett and Hale, The Last Voyage of the Karluk (Small, Maynard, 1916)
creator: drawn for the narrative
description: The published chart of the drift, with three separate lines keyed in the legend: the Karluk's drift, the drift of the ice-floe camp, and the track of Captain Bartlett - Wrangel Island, Herald Island, the Siberian coast and the Alaskan shore all marked. It is the single most useful image for reconstructing the whole disaster.

title: Coastal profile views: Cape Penrhyn and the mouth of the Strait of the Fury and Hecla
credit: Parry, Journal of a Second Voyage for the Discovery of a North-West Passage (London: John Murray, 1824); scan Internet Archive
creator: G. F. Lyon (artist)
description: Further strips from the folding plate of coastal profiles, labelled with Cape Penrhyn and the mouth of the Strait of the Fury and Hecla, the strait Parry's ships tried and failed to force in 1822.

title: Coastal profile views: Liddon Island, the Narrows, and the Strait of the Fury and Hecla
credit: Parry, Journal of a Second Voyage for the Discovery of a North-West Passage (London: John Murray, 1824); scan Internet Archive
creator: G. F. Lyon (artist)
description: Coastal-profile strips labelled Liddon Island, the Narrows seen from east and west, and views of the Strait of the Fury and Hecla taken from Whyte Inlet and from Fire Rock -- the innermost part of the strait that blocked Parry's passage west.

title: General Chart shewing the track of H.M. Ships Fury and Hecla, on a voyage for the discovery of a North-West Passage, 1821-22-23
credit: Parry, Journal of a Second Voyage for the Discovery of a North-West Passage (London: John Murray, 1824); scan Internet Archive
creator: John Walker (engraver)
description: The volume's summary chart of the whole voyage, plotting the ships' track from Hudson Strait through Foxe Basin to Igloolik and the Strait of the Fury and Hecla against the wider geography from Baffin Bay to Hudson Bay, with the coasts newly charted by this and the preceding expedition shaded to show what had been added to the map. It was engraved for William Edward Parry's journal of the second voyage.

title: Fig. 10 -- Eastern Arctic region location map
credit: Usher 1971, Fur Trade Posts of the Northwest Territories 1870-1970 (Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, Northern Science Research Group 71-4)
description: Location map of the Eastern Arctic region (Region 5), captioned 'FIG. 10 EASTERN ARCTIC REGION LOCATION MAP', covering Baffin Island, the Foxe Basin coast, Devon and Ellesmere islands and northern Quebec, divided into four numbered subregions: 5A South Baffin, 5B East Baffin, 5C North Baffin, 5D High Arctic, with numbered trading-site dots keyed to Table 8 (e.g. 1 Resolute, 3/4 Grise Fiord/Craig Harbour, 6 Arctic Bay, 10 Igloolik, 5 Pond Inlet area, Frobisher Bay, Lake Harbour, Cape Dorset, Pangnirtung, Cumberland Sound). Covers the whole eastern Arctic; coordinates given are a rough regional centre.

title: Fig. 9 -- Western Arctic region location map
credit: Usher 1971, Fur Trade Posts of the Northwest Territories 1870-1970 (Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, Northern Science Research Group 71-4)
description: Location map captioned 'FIG. 9 WESTERN ARCTIC REGION LOCATION MAP' (this figure's own caption reads Western Arctic, though the facing Table 7 is titled Arctic Coast Region -- both name Region 4), covering the Yukon/Beaufort coast, Amundsen Gulf, Victoria Island, Coronation Gulf and Queen Maud Gulf, divided into three numbered subregions: 4A Beaufort, 4B Coronation, 4C Queen Maud, with numbered site dots including Tuktoyaktuk, Coppermine, Cambridge Bay, Holman, Gjoa Haven, Spence Bay and Pelly Bay. Covers the whole western Arctic coast; coordinates given are a rough regional centre.

title: Arctic Regions, Showing Location of Circumpolar Stations, 1881-83
credit: Greely, Three Years of Arctic Service (Scribner, 1886), vol. I; engraved from photographs by Sergeant George W. Rice
description: Polar-projection map printed opposite Greely's account of the first International Polar Year, with the eleven circumpolar stations joined by a ring of straight lines and Lockwood's 1882 farthest marked north of Greenland. Coordinates given are a point in the area the map centres on; the map itself is circumpolar.

title: Replica of the Erebus bell at the Nattilik Heritage Centre
credit: Kerry Raymond, 7 September 2019; Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
creator: Kerry Raymond
description: A replica, on display in the community's own heritage centre at Uqsuqtuuq, of the ship's bell recovered from HMS Erebus; the year 1845 is visible near the top. The photographer's own caption calls it a replica. The wreck was found in 2014 in Wilmot and Crampton Bay after Netsilik oral testimony - gathered over a lifetime by Louie Kamookak of this hamlet and, before him, by Rae, Hall, Schwatka and Amundsen - put the searchers in the right water. The object sits in Gjoa Haven, in the hamlet named for Amundsen's ship, which is why it belongs to this topic as well as to franklin-1845 and wrecks-disasters.

title: RMS Nascopie, the ship that tied the eastern Arctic together
credit: Hudson's Bay Company Archives, Archives of Manitoba: Nascopie ship history sheet
licence: Crown copyright, Province of Manitoba; reproduced for research
creator: Swan Hunter and Wigham Richardson, Neptune Works, Wallsend-on-Tyne
description: A steel screw semi-icebreaker of 2,520 gross tons, 285 feet long, built at Wallsend-on-Tyne in 1911-12 for the Nascopie Steamship Company, a joint venture of the Hudson's Bay Company and Job Brothers of St John's. She carried fifty passengers and forty-five to fifty crew and made twelve to thirteen knots. For thirty-five years she was the one annual link between the eastern Arctic posts and the south: she supplied the trading posts, worked the Newfoundland seal fishery, ran French government cargoes to the White Sea in the First World War, brought a reindeer herd and its Sami herders from Norway to Baffin Island in 1921, carried the government's Eastern Arctic Patrol from 1933, and in 1937 made a combined transit of the Northwest Passage with the MS Aklavik. Thomas Smellie commanded her longer than anyone, 1917-19, 1922-25 and 1933-45. She struck an uncharted reef at the entrance to Kinngait (Cape Dorset) harbour on 21 July 1947; everyone got off, and a storm on 15 October carried what was left of her away.

title: The St. Roch herself, at Kitsilano Point
credit: Parks Canada Agency, Directory of Federal Heritage Designations
creator: Burrard Dry Dock Company, North Vancouver
description: A 31.6-metre auxiliary schooner of 323 tons displacement, Douglas fir sheathed in Australian ironbark, designed by Charles Druguid and Thomas Halliday and built in 1928 for the RCMP. She spent eleven winters in the Arctic. Designated a National Historic Site on 15 May 1962 and preserved dry, under an A-frame at the Vancouver Maritime Museum, restored to her appearance in 1944.

title: CCGS Amundsen: the Coast Guard's own record of the ship
credit: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, CCG Fleet vessel details; Crown copyright
creator: Canadian Coast Guard
description: Medium icebreaker, Arctic Class 3, 98.2 m long, 19.5 m in the beam, 7.2 m draught, 5,911 gross tonnes; six Alco M251F diesels driving two fixed-pitch propellers through a diesel-electric plant of 10,142 kW; 35,000 nautical miles' range, 100 days' endurance; complement 31 with 51 berths; helicopter hangar and flight deck; a moon pool with an ROV control room and geology and nutrient laboratories. Built by Burrard Dry Dock and in service since 1979; home port Quebec. Pinned at Quebec, her home port.

title: The Resolute desk
credit: The White House (photograph, 2021), via Wikimedia Commons
creator: made at Chatham Dockyard from the timbers of HMS Resolute
description: A desk made from the timbers of the ship Kellett was ordered to abandon in Barrow Strait on 15 May 1854, and which then sailed herself twelve hundred miles to Davis Strait. Queen Victoria had it made after the Resolute was broken up in 1879 and gave it to President Hayes in 1880; it stands in the Oval Office. Of everything the Franklin search produced, this is the object most people have seen. The photograph is a White House one of 2021, showing the carved front panel.

title: Kood-lin and Ik-ku-mer, the Stone Lamp and Fire of the Esquimaux
credit: Hall, Life with the Esquimaux (London: Sampson Low, 1864); scan Internet Archive
creator: Charles Parsons and others, after an implement collected by the author
description: A soapstone oil lamp and its wooden drying frame, the all-purpose Inuit lamp Hall describes as giving heat, light, and cooking fire during the long Arctic winter night.

title: Ek-ke-lu-yun, the White-Stone Salmon-Bait Used by Esquimaux
credit: Hall, Life with the Esquimaux (London: Sampson Low, 1864); scan Internet Archive
creator: Charles Parsons and others, after an implement collected by the author
description: A carved white-stone lure used by Inuit fishermen to attract salmon, drawn from a specimen Hall obtained; he notes it was made with exceptional craftsmanship.

title: Head and Antlers of the Arctic Reindeer
credit: Hall, Life with the Esquimaux (London: Sampson Low, 1864); scan Internet Archive
creator: Charles Parsons and others, after a specimen collected by the author
description: A mounted reindeer head and antlers shown as a natural-history specimen, illustrating the caribou hunted by Hall's Inuit companions for food and skins.

title: Hunt's St. Michael Sledge. Relief Expedition, 1884
credit: Greely, Three Years of Arctic Service (Scribner, 1886), vol. I; engraved from photographs by Sergeant George W. Rice
description: The Alaskan sledge pattern Greely recommends to future explorers in high latitudes, with steel runners that can be attached or detached at pleasure. He judges the Hudson Bay and St Michael sledges, at about thirty-five pounds each, lighter on the men than the rigid mortised-and-riveted McClintock sledge, which cannot stay long unbroken over rough ice.

title: An Arctic Wolf, killed near Fort Conger
credit: Greely, Three Years of Arctic Service (Scribner, 1886), vol. I; engraved from photographs by Sergeant George W. Rice
creator: Sergeant George W. Rice, photographer of the expedition
description: A white wolf laid out on the shingle, from a photograph. The facing text records the party's only close encounter with a live one: Private Henry reported that on entering the tunnel of the snow-house a huge wolf met him and escaped by running over his back, and Connell met a wolf between Cape Beechey and Depot B.
